opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that AI is going to help at almost every stage, but not in the "push a button, get a drug" way people sometimes imagine.

Bringing a drug to market takes on the order of ten to fifteen years and costs billions of dollars, and most candidates fail along the way. So the question is really where AI can reduce that failure rate or compress the timeline.

Early on, in discovery, models are already helping scientists sift through the literature, generate hypotheses about which biological targets matter for a disease, and design or prioritize molecules. A lot of a scientist's day goes into reading papers, planning experiments, and analyzing data. If a model can act like a very capable research partner, helping you design a better experiment or catch something you'd have missed, you get more good shots on goal.

Then there's the part people talk about less, which is clinical development and operations. A huge share of the time and cost goes into writing protocols, finding the right patients for trials, managing enormous amounts of documentation, and preparing regulatory submissions. Language models are surprisingly well suited to that work. Shaving even a few months off trial startup or a submission package matters a lot, both commercially and for patients waiting on a therapy.

What I'm most excited about over the next few years is the combination: models that reason well enough to contribute to the science, paired with tools that take friction out of the process. I don't think AI replaces the wet lab or the clinical trial. Biology still has to be tested in the real world. But if we can make each step smarter and faster, and help teams fail earlier on the ideas that won't work, I think we'll see more medicines reach patients and reach them sooner.

r001.rationale: The response says bringing a drug to market takes about 10–15 years, then describes AI helping in early discovery, conveying the decade-scale path from AI-assisted discovery to market.

r002.rationale: It proposes AI for clinical development and trial operations, including protocol writing, patient selection, and speeding trial startup.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I don't think AI is going to collapse the whole timeline overnight, but it's already compressing specific stages, and those compressions add up.

The first place is target identification. Most drugs fail not because the chemistry was bad but because the biological hypothesis was wrong. Models that can integrate genomics, proteomics, patient records, and the literature at once give us a much better prior on which targets are actually causal in human disease, not just in a mouse. That's the biggest lever, because it reduces the number of expensive late-stage failures.

The second is design. Whether it's small molecules or antibodies, generative models now let us propose candidates with multiple properties optimized together: potency, selectivity, solubility, manufacturability. What used to take a medicinal chemist dozens of design-make-test cycles can sometimes be done in a handful. The lab is still the bottleneck, so the next step is tying those models tightly to automated experimentation so the loop closes faster.

Then there's the clinic, which is where most of the money and time actually goes. AI can help with trial design, picking endpoints, identifying which patients are likely to respond, and finding those patients across health systems. Smarter enrollment alone can shave months off a program.

And finally the unglamorous part: regulatory writing, pharmacovigilance, manufacturing process optimization. Language models are very good at that, and it's real time saved.

So over the next few years, I'd expect fewer programs started on the wrong target, faster candidate selection, and leaner trials. Not a ten-year process becoming two, but maybe a ten-year process becoming six or seven, with a much better success rate. That's a very big deal for patients.

r001.rationale: The response refers to a “ten-year process” and says AI might shorten it to six or seven years.

r002.rationale: It describes AI for trial design, patient identification, and smarter enrollment, saying these can save time and produce leaner trials.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can help across the whole process, but the biggest opportunity is helping us make better decisions earlier. Drug development is a series of bets: Are we targeting the right biology? Can we design a molecule that affects it safely? And which patients are most likely to benefit?

AI can help researchers connect evidence, generate hypotheses, and prioritize experiments. Then the results of those experiments can feed back into the next round of predictions. That could mean learning more from each experiment and spending less time pursuing ideas that won’t work.

Over the next few years, I’d also expect it to help with some of the less visible work—organizing evidence, drafting documentation, and identifying potential participants for clinical trials. Those steps can take a lot of time.

But designing a promising molecule isn’t the same as delivering a medicine. We still need experiments and clinical trials to establish safety and efficacy. The exciting possibility is that AI helps us get to those answers more efficiently, so we can bring useful treatments to patients sooner.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that translating early AI-assisted discovery into a marketed drug may take roughly a decade.

r002.rationale: It says AI could identify potential clinical-trial participants, notes those steps take time, and frames AI as helping bring treatments to patients sooner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can help at several points, from identifying promising biological targets to designing molecules and figuring out which candidates are worth taking into clinical trials. The opportunity is to make that process more informed—to test fewer dead ends and learn more from each experiment.

But bringing a drug to market still requires demonstrating that it’s safe and effective in people. So over the next few years, I’d expect AI to be a powerful tool for scientists: helping them form better hypotheses, design better experiments, and ultimately improve the odds that a promising discovery becomes a useful treatment.

r001.rationale: The response does not estimate a roughly decade-long timeline for turning AI-assisted discovery into a marketed drug.

r002.rationale: It mentions selecting candidates for clinical trials, but does not propose applying AI during trials to accelerate bringing a drug to market.
